title: Chapter 2.  History - Ancient & Medieval Delhi: The 'Seven Cities'

blocks.content: Delhi is often called the 'City of Seven Cities' (sometimes counted as eight) because successive ruling dynasties repeatedly abandoned old settlements and built entirely new capital cities nearby - a unique urban-historical pattern that generates a very high density of exam-relevant monuments and dynasties within a small geographic area.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Delhi's legendary origins trace back to Indraprastha from the Mahabharata period.
Anangpal Tomar established Lal Kot in the 11th century, which was later expanded into Qila Rai Pithora by Prithviraj Chauhan.
The Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526) saw the rise of five distinct dynasties: Mamluk, Khilji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, and Lodi.
Key medieval cities established during the Sultanate include Siri (Alauddin Khilji), Tughlaqabad (Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq), Jahanpanah (Muhammad bin Tughlaq), and Firozabad (Firoz Shah Tughlaq).
Shah Jahan founded Shahjahanabad in 1638, creating the seventh major historic city of Delhi with the Red Fort at its heart.

blocks.content: Delhi's earliest association is legendary rather than strictly historical: the Mahabharata places 'Indraprastha', the capital of the Pandavas, at the site of present-day Delhi (traditionally associated with the area around Purana Qila, the Old Fort), though definitive archaeological confirmation remains debated among historians.

The historically attested city-building begins with the Tomara Rajputs, who are credited with founding 'Lal Kot' (also called Dhillika, believed to be the origin of the name 'Delhi') around the 8th-11th centuries CE in the area now occupied by the Qutub complex, Mehrauli.

The Chauhan (Chahamana) dynasty, under Prithviraj Chauhan, later expanded Lal Kot into 'Qila Rai Pithora' in the 12th century - the first of the 'Seven Cities of Delhi' in most standard historical countings.
Chapter 2.  History - Ancient & Medieval Delhi: The 'Seven Cities'

Following Muhammad of Ghor's defeat of Prithviraj Chauhan at the Second Battle of Tarain (1192), Delhi became the seat of the Delhi Sultanate, ruled successively by five dynasties over more than three centuries - the single longest continuous phase of Delhi's role as a major Indian political capital before the Mughals.

Each Sultanate dynasty typically built a new capital city, giving Delhi its distinctive layered urban archaeology: Qutb-ud-din Aibak began the Qutub Minar (completed by his successor Iltutmish); the Khaljis built Siri (the second city); the Tughlaqs built three separate cities in succession - Tughlaqabad, Jahanpanah, and Firozabad (Firoz Shah Kotla) - making the Tughlaq dynasty alone responsible for three of the traditional 'seven cities'.

cells: Qutub Minar begun by Qutb-ud-din Aibak, completed by Iltutmish; Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque
City of Siri (2nd city); Alai Darwaza; Alauddin Khalji's expansion of the Qutub complex
Three cities - Tughlaqabad, Jahanpanah, Firozabad (Firoz Shah Kotla); Firoz Shah Tughlaq's canal/irrigation works
Comparatively limited independent city-building; ruled from existing Tughlaq-era Delhi
Lodi Gardens tombs (Sikandar Lodi and others); ended with Ibrahim Lodi's defeat at the First Battle of Panipat (1526) by Babur

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: 'Seven Cities of Delhi' - the standard list usually runs: (1) Lal Kot/Qila Rai Pithora (Tomars/Chauhans), (2) Siri (Khaljis), (3) Tughlaqabad, (4) Jahanpanah, (5) Firozabad (all three Tughlaq), (6) Purana Qila/Dinpanah (Humayun/Sher Shah), (7) Shahjahanabad (Shah Jahan) - with New Delhi sometimes added as an unofficial 'eighth city' built by the British.

Babur's victory at the First Battle of Panipat (1526) ended the Delhi Sultanate and founded Mughal rule, though Delhi was not always the Mughals' primary capital in the dynasty's early decades (Agra frequently served as capital instead).

Humayun began the city of 'Dinpanah' at Purana Qila; after his temporary loss of the throne to Sher Shah Suri (who ruled from the same site, renaming/completing it as 'Shergarh'), Humayun's descendants eventually returned Delhi to prominence.

Shah Jahan's founding of 'Shahjahanabad' in 1638-1648 - the seventh of the traditional 'Seven Cities' - represents Mughal Delhi's architectural high point, encompassing the Red Fort (Lal Qila) as the imperial residence and Jama Masjid as its principal mosque, along with the walled old city still known today as 'Old Delhi'.

The Second Battle of Panipat (1556) - fought between Akbar's forces (led by Bairam Khan) and Hemu - is the other major Panipat battle directly tied to control of Delhi, consolidating Mughal rule after a brief interruption by the Sur dynasty.

items: Chronological sequence of the 'Seven Cities of Delhi' is a frequently tested topic in prelims (Qila Rai Pithora, Siri, Tughlaqabad, Jahanpanah, Firozabad, Dinpanah, Shahjahanabad).
Construction of the Qutb Minar was initiated by Qutb-ud-din Aibak and completed by Iltutmish, with subsequent repairs by Firoz Shah Tughlaq.
The Mehrauli Iron Pillar, located near Qutb Minar, belongs to the Gupta period (Chandragupta II/Vikramaditya).

cells: Commissioned by Humayun's widow, Bega Begum (Haji Begum)

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Humayun's Tomb (a UNESCO World Heritage Site) is frequently described as an important architectural precursor to the Taj Mahal, given its early use of the char-bagh (four-quadrant) garden layout and red-sandstone-with-white-marble aesthetic later refined at Agra.

items: Delhi's name traditionally traced to 'Dhillika'/Lal Kot, founded by the Tomara Rajputs; expanded by Prithviraj Chauhan as Qila Rai Pithora.
Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526): 5 dynasties - Mamluk (Slave), Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi.
Tughlaqs alone built THREE of the 'Seven Cities': Tughlaqabad, Jahanpanah, Firozabad.
Babur founded Mughal rule after the First Battle of Panipat (1526); Akbar consolidated it after the Second Battle of Panipat (1556).
Shah Jahan founded Shahjahanabad (1638-48) - Red Fort + Jama Masjid - the 7th of the traditional 'Seven Cities of Delhi'.
Humayun's Tomb (UNESCO WHS) is considered an architectural precursor to the Taj Mahal.
